title: Creating tokens in Dash Evolution: a conversation

teacher.name: Chad G. P. Taylor
teacher.delivery: Natural male English voice; relaxed, mildly know-it-all; humor only at his own expense.

learner.name: Ewa Dashwood
learner.delivery: Natural female English voice; inquisitive, thoughtful, conversational; no caricature.

packaging.standalone: Each part intro, its scenes, then its outro.
packaging.combined: All 54 scenes in order; omit part intro/outro extras to avoid repeated bridges.
packaging.recording_gate: Independent scenario audit and observed GUI outcomes required before full recording.
packaging.spoken_content: Only turns, part intro and part outro are spoken. Screen plans and controls are production metadata.

intro.speaker: teacher
intro.text: Start here: prepare a testnet identity, configure a simple token, and verify its registration.

outro.speaker: learner
outro.text: Keep the final identifiers. Next, we will examine advanced settings and who may change the rules.

intro.speaker: learner
intro.text: This part begins a fresh CloudPoint draft: names, precision, transferability, histories, and the structure of permissions.

outro.speaker: teacher
outro.text: Keep this as a draft. Next comes each action, its consequences, and a small group example.

intro.speaker: teacher
intro.text: Continue the CloudPoint draft with supply limits, mint destinations, intervention powers, and group authority.

outro.speaker: learner
outro.text: Our practice group is removed. Next, we will compare recurring distribution recipes without publishing them.

intro.speaker: learner
intro.text: This part compares all eight recurring emission functions. Keep the base-unit tables beside the draft.

outro.speaker: teacher
outro.text: Recurring rules are locked and the feature is off. Next: scheduled allocations, document schemas, and JSON.

intro.speaker: teacher
intro.text: We continue with scheduled and once-per-identity allocations, then inspect document schemas and the contract preview.

outro.speaker: learner
outro.text: The practice features are cleared. The final part reviews authority, registers CloudPoint, and checks the result.

intro.speaker: learner
intro.text: Use this final part with the reviewed CloudPoint draft. We will verify permissions before confirming registration.

outro.speaker: teacher
outro.text: Keep your confirmed identifiers and reviewed configuration. Revisit the relevant chapter before changing your next draft.

scenes.title: Welcome from Chad
scenes.screen: Official opening slide. Display Chad G. P. Taylor (teacher) and Ewa Dashwood (learner). Discreet AI-generated narration disclosure.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Hello, I'm Chad G. P. Taylor. We're going to create tokens in Dash Evolution, starting with a simple example and working through the advanced controls.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I'm Ewa Dashwood. I'd like to understand the choices, especially the ones I can't change afterward. Can we build something small before tackling all the permissions?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Absolutely. We'll register a small token, then examine a more detailed example. I'll explain the switches as we reach them. My confidence may arrive slightly ahead of the explanation.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I'll keep an eye on both. Let's start with what the token creator actually does.

scenes.title: What this lesson covers
scenes.screen: Chapter overview. Basic token; advanced settings; permissions; groups; distribution recipes; documents; final review.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Are we registering every example we try, or working toward one final configuration?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Two registrations: a simple fixed-supply token first, then our final advanced token. Between them, we'll experiment with permissions, groups, distribution recipes, and document schemas without publishing those practice settings.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So I can explore a panel without committing to its features?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Opening a panel doesn't enable its features, and editing a draft doesn't publish it. We will distinguish each experiment from the final settings.

scenes.title: Prepare the right account
scenes.screen: Settings on Testnet; green connection status. Identity home showing funded identity. No recovery phrases or private key screens.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: First, check Testnet in Settings and wait for synchronization. We need a funded Platform identity with an available Authentication key at High or Critical security level.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does having its public identity identifier satisfy that requirement?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No, we also need the ability to sign. If that key comes from a wallet, import and unlock the wallet beforehand, with recording stopped.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What if I imported an identity with its own available private key?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: You don't need a separate wallet merely to register this contract. Wallet setup, identity funding, and secret handling happen before this lesson. We'll show the prepared public state, never recovery phrases or private keys.

scenes.title: Find the token workspace
scenes.screen: Tokens sidebar; My Tokens, Search Tokens, Token Creator. Hover help icons; top Refresh, Import Token and Create Token only where present.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Tokens has several destinations. Which one creates something new?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Token Creator, or the Create Token shortcut. My Tokens lists tokens you track; Search Tokens helps find existing contracts. Import Token takes an existing token identifier. It doesn't create a token.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And Refresh updates the information already on screen?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It fetches current information. We'll use it when checking results. The small information buttons explain nearby fields, and we can open those as reminders. We'll also check what the settings actually do, because a short tooltip cannot describe every consequence. For now, choose Token Creator and leave the advanced options closed.

scenes.title: A simple token: identity and name
scenes.screen: Simple creator, Advanced off. Explicitly select funded identity. Enter CloudCredit and a short description.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Select the funded identity inside this form. It will own the contract. With Show Advanced Options off, the app selects a suitable available signing key for us.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If the list is empty, is Load Identity the next step?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes, it opens the import flow; complete that separately before continuing. For our prepared identity, enter CloudCredit as one word and the description, A fixed-supply token for learning.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does the description enforce that policy?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. Permissions enforce it. Names and descriptions explain the token; they aren't unique identifiers or promises of value. We'll configure the actual supply next.

scenes.title: Initial and maximum supply
scenes.screen: Initial Supply 1000, Max Supply 1000. Point to token amount inputs, not identity DASH balance.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Both fields say supply. What happens if I put one thousand in each?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Initial Supply creates one thousand tokens when registration succeeds. Max Supply sets a ceiling of one thousand under the rules we choose. These inputs use displayed token amounts, including fractions you enter; they aren't Dash amounts or raw base units.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Could I leave the maximum blank if I haven't decided?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: An empty maximum, or zero where this form treats it as no maximum, leaves no numerical ceiling. For CloudCredit, enter one thousand in both fields. We'll also remove future minting authority, so the ceiling and permissions agree.

scenes.title: Presets in plain English
scenes.screen: Open the five-entry simple preset menu. Show the full thirteen-rule preset comparison matrix from the inventory, including performers, administrators and flags; highlight the extra Minting and Burning powers. Select Most Restrictive for CloudCredit.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Presets fill in permission bundles. Most Restrictive disables additional actions and administrators. Only Emergency Action adds pause and resume.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does Minting and Burning grant exactly those two powers?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: More than its name suggests: owner emergency control, convention changes, destination-policy changes, marketplace mode changes, and direct-purchase pricing too. The comparison table shows the full bundle.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What do Advanced Actions and All Allowed add?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Advanced Actions grants broader owner powers, including freeze, destruction of frozen balances, and maximum-supply changes. All Allowed also makes later rule changes more permissive. We'll inspect performers, administrators, and switches in Advanced Options. For CloudCredit, choose Most Restrictive.

scenes.title: What fixed means here
scenes.screen: Most Restrictive selected. Create Token enabled.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: With Most Restrictive, could the owner turn minting back on after registration?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Those extra powers and their administrators are disabled. They can't simply be enabled later. Together with initial and maximum supply of one thousand, that gives this example its fixed configuration.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I only entered a singular name. Where does the plural come from?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Simple mode supplies it from the singular. For deliberate plural forms, translations, or custom permissions, use Advanced Options before registering. We're choosing the simple version deliberately, rather than postponing a decision the contract may lock permanently.

scenes.title: Review and register the simple token
scenes.screen: Click Create Token, read actual confirmation. Explain marketplace warning and displayed estimated cost. Confirm once; wait on observed state, not a scheduled delay.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Click Create Token and compare the name, both supplies, and estimated registration cost with our plan.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: The cost is displayed in Dash. Is that a separate wallet payment?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It comes from this identity's Platform credits; Dash is the displayed equivalent. The estimate isn't an exact receipt. Also read the permanent marketplace warning: it concerns marketplace sales, not ordinary transfers between holders.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If something differs, Cancel takes me back to editing?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Otherwise, Confirm once and wait for the observed result. We won't treat a slow response as an invitation to submit another paid registration.

scenes.title: Verify the result and keep the identifiers
scenes.screen: Observed success; My Tokens; token balance; More Info with full Token ID and Contract ID. Highlight Back/reset separately.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Once success is confirmed, what should I check independently?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Open My Tokens, select CloudCredit, and inspect the balance. For this example, the creator identity should receive one thousand tokens. More Info shows the full Token ID and Contract ID; save both after registration.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Why not just save the name or an earlier preview?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Different tokens can share a display name, and the preview doesn't substitute for final identifiers. We're checking the actual registered result. The success screen's Back button resets the creator form for another example. We'll use a fresh form for CloudPoint and its custom permissions.

scenes.title: Start the advanced example
scenes.screen: Open fresh creator; enable Advanced. Explicitly select identity and available Authentication High/Critical key. Show eligible key selector without revealing private bytes.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Open a fresh creator and enable Show Advanced Options. Check the selected identity again, then choose an eligible Authentication key at High or Critical security level.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Are we exposing private-key material in this selector?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No, it lists identity keys, not their private bytes. A disabled key or one with the wrong purpose won't do. Unlock the relevant wallet separately if needed.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Will every setting we demonstrate remain in CloudPoint?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. We'll try some alternatives, then reset them to a specific final plan. Keep that distinction in mind throughout: a configuration experiment is useful precisely because we haven't published it yet.

scenes.title: Names, plural forms, and translations
scenes.screen: Enter CloudPoint / CloudPoints in English. Add Polish localization Punkt / Punkty. Remove the added localization after demonstrating. Use language menu and remove-language control.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Here I can choose the plural explicitly. Let's use CloudPoint and CloudPoints.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: In the English row, yes. Add Language creates another localization. Choose Polish and enter Punkt and Punkty for a small example. Avoid duplicate entries for the same language.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does that give Polish users a different token or balance?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No, those are names for the same token and supply. The remove control deletes an extra localization from the draft. We'll remove the practice translation and keep English for our final example.

scenes.title: Supply, keywords, and description
scenes.screen: Base Supply 1000, Max Supply 10000. Additional keywords field blank; briefly enter then remove education. Description filled.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Base Supply is the advanced form's initial supply. Set one thousand, then set Max Supply to ten thousand. We'll make that ceiling permanent through its permissions later.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If Contract Keywords is blank, is the token unsearchable?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. This build still registers the singular name as a searchable keyword and counts it in the estimate. Try education as an additional keyword, then remove it for our final setup.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So an extra keyword adds discovery information and another keyword charge?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. Add a short, honest description too.

scenes.title: Decimal places and the base-unit conversion
scenes.screen: Expand Advanced; Max Decimals 2. Recheck supply fields after precision change. Overlay: 1 token = 100 base units; 1000 = 100000 base units.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What does setting Max Decimals to two change?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: One token represents one hundred base units; the smallest unit is one hundredth of a token. Zero decimals would mean indivisible whole tokens.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Should I divide our supply entries by a hundred now?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. After changing precision, recheck that the displayed fields still read one thousand and ten thousand. The form scales them for you. JSON will later show one hundred thousand and one million base units.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So the different numbers describe the same amounts.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Correct. We'll be especially careful when distribution fields ask for base units directly.

scenes.title: Pause and transferability
scenes.screen: Show Start as paused and Holders can send this token to other identities, with info icons. Label transferability Permanent after registration. Demonstrate draft-only toggles, restoring paused off / transferable on. If unsupported, show the protocol explanation rather than enabling an invalid configuration.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Start as paused controls the initial transfer state. If we use it, someone needs Emergency Action authority to resume transfers later.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Is unchecking Holders can send this token to other identities another kind of pause?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. Transferability can change in the draft, but it cannot change after registration. Creating a non-transferable token requires a known supported protocol version of at least fourteen.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So I mustn't publish it expecting an unpause button to restore transfers.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. If the option is unavailable, read its explanation rather than bypassing it. Our final token starts unpaused, with ordinary transfers enabled.

scenes.title: History ledgers and capitalization
scenes.screen: Keep history parent checkbox; Advanced [+]; all six child toggles, mixed parent state, restore all enabled. Name should be capitalized checkbox.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does Keep history mean the app stores records only on this computer?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It's a contract configuration choice, not a local privacy switch. Expand Advanced to see six ledgers: transfers, freezes and unfreezes, mints, burns, direct-pricing changes, and direct purchases.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can a payment token retain transfers while choosing other ledgers separately?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. A token with direct sales may also need pricing and purchase records. The parent checkbox changes all six; a mixed state means only some are selected. We'll keep all six enabled.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And Name should be capitalized?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Presentation guidance for clients. It doesn't change the identifier or add a localization.

scenes.title: Advanced presets are authority bundles
scenes.screen: Action Rules; preset selector including Custom. Highlight Advanced Actions, All Allowed and Custom; use practice preset and inspect key rows.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Open Action Rules. The preset selector includes Custom, where we choose rules ourselves.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If I select another preset after editing, will it preserve my individual changes?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Don't assume so; it can overwrite them. Compare the full permission table first. Advanced Actions includes substantial owner authority, such as changing the supply ceiling and destroying frozen balances. All Allowed permits broader changes to the authorities themselves.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So the useful comparison is who can do what, and who can change that arrangement.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Precisely. We'll inspect both, then customize our final setup.

scenes.title: Who performs an action
scenes.screen: Expand Manual Mint. Show No One / Contract Owner / Identity; enter a valid public identity ID and explain format validation. Point out No Groups Added Yet. Defer Main Group / Group 0 selection to scene 29. Restore owner.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: In Manual Mint, what does Authorized to perform action select?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Its performer. No One disables the action. Contract Owner gives it to the identity owning the contract. Identity names a particular identity using its complete Base58 identifier.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does the validation check mark prove that I control the identity?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Only that the identifier has the expected format. It doesn't prove possession of its keys. A treasury identity could be our minting authority, for example.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I see No Groups Added Yet rather than a group choice.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Those choices appear once a group exists. We'll return to Main Group and Group zero after creating one.

scenes.title: Who may change the rule
scenes.screen: Authorized to change rules selector and all three boolean switches. Use an example before/after diagram, not a signed update.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If a group performs minting but the owner can change its rule, is the group really the final authority?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The owner may still change that arrangement. That's why Authorized to change rules matters separately from the performer.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What do these three switches constrain?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The first allows changing the performer to No One, potentially disabling the action permanently. The second allows changing the administrator to No One, locking future rule updates. The third allows an administrator to change its own administrator assignment.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: They don't grant those actions to everybody?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. They constrain later authorized updates. Decide both selectors and all three switches before registration.

scenes.title: Make the supply ceiling genuinely permanent
scenes.screen: Expand Max Supply Change. Set performer No One, administrator No One, and all three rule-change switches off. Show the final 10000 supply cap in the summary.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: We entered a maximum of ten thousand. Which permission makes it a permanent ceiling?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Max Supply Change. Set both its performer and administrator to No One, with later rule-change switches off. A numerical maximum alone isn't a promise that nobody can revise it.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can the owner still mint below that ceiling?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes, if Manual Mint permits it. Those are separate decisions. A project needing an adjustable ceiling should instead choose and disclose who can change it. Our CloudPoint example deliberately fixes ten thousand.

scenes.title: Minting and the mint destination
scenes.screen: Set Manual Mint performer Contract Owner, administrator No One. Demonstrate default-to-owner, a specific public treasury identity, and per-mint destination choice. Leave the specific-default-identity option enabled through the start of scene 21 so its nested rule remains visible.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Set Manual Mint to Contract Owner, with its administrator No One. The owner could issue ten reward tokens after a completed task, within the supply ceiling.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Where would those new tokens go?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The destination settings choose the owner, a specified default identity, or a recipient chosen per mint when allowed. A treasury is a useful example of a specific default.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does that default affect only future mints?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It can also affect the initial allocation. We'll leave the specific treasury option visible briefly to inspect its nested rule. Then we'll lock that rule and restore the owner as our final default.

scenes.title: Destination rule changes
scenes.screen: While Use a default identity to receive newly minted tokens is enabled, set New Tokens Destination Identity Rules performer No One, administrator No One, all three switches false. Then restore default-to-owner. Leave per-mint recipient choice enabled. In Minting Allow Choosing Destination Rules set both selectors No One and all three switches false. Keep these final values.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Why lock the destination rule before switching the default back to the owner?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: New Tokens Destination Identity Rules is visible only while the specific-identity option is enabled. Set its performer and administrator to No One, and all three switches off. Then restore the owner as default.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Otherwise the hidden rule could retain permission to change that policy?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Hiding a panel doesn't reset its values. Now leave per-mint recipient choice enabled, but set both selectors in Minting Allow Choosing Destination Rules to No One, with all three switches off.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: We allow choosing a recipient, while locking who can revise that capability.

scenes.title: Burning is not confiscation
scenes.screen: Manual Burn rule. Owner performer and No One admin for final sample. Illustrative balance 100→90 and supply 1000→990.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: With Manual Burn, could the owner remove tokens from any holder?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: This burn action reduces the executing identity's own balance and current supply. An authorized identity holding one hundred tokens could burn ten, leaving ninety. If total supply was one thousand, it becomes nine hundred ninety.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: That's different from sending ten tokens somewhere recoverable.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. Burning isn't a transfer to a recovery account, and you shouldn't expect an undo. Destroying another frozen identity's balance is a separate power, which we'll examine shortly. For CloudPoint, allow the owner to burn its own tokens and set the administrator to No One.

scenes.title: Freeze and unfreeze
scenes.screen: Freeze, allow transfers to frozen identities, Unfreeze. Explain with a paused membership-account example. Restore both action and admin No One in final sample.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Freeze prevents a particular identity from sending this token. The accompanying checkbox decides whether that frozen identity can still receive transfers.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So a project could suspend outgoing account activity while allowing incoming tokens, or block those too?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Unfreeze is a separate permission that restores the relevant ability to move tokens. Don't assume whoever may freeze automatically has permission to unfreeze.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Would our final token allow either intervention?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. We'll demonstrate both settings and the incoming-transfer checkbox, then set the freeze and unfreeze performers and administrators to No One.

scenes.title: Destroying frozen funds
scenes.screen: Destroy Frozen Funds action and admin. Explicit whole-balance diagram. Restore both No One. Explain difference from All Allowed / Advanced Actions presets.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: How much can Destroy Frozen Funds remove from a frozen identity?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Its entire balance of this token. An authorized controller targets another frozen identity; there isn't a field here for selecting a small partial amount.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And unfreezing afterward wouldn't restore those tokens?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Correct. This is destruction, not a temporary hold. Advanced Actions grants the power to the owner, which is why we inspected the preset rather than relying on its friendly name.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: We don't need that authority for our example.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Then both selectors stay No One. Any project that does need it should explain the consequence plainly to holders beforehand.

scenes.title: Emergency actions and convention changes
scenes.screen: Emergency Action owner performer / No One admin; Conventions Change No One / No One. Briefly indicate decimals and localization protected by conventions rule.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Emergency Action is token-wide pause and resume. A project might use it while investigating an operational problem.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Unlike Freeze, which singles out an identity?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. Our final configuration keeps emergency authority with the owner and locks its administrator. Conventions Change is different again: it concerns naming and decimal conventions.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Could a convention change affect how balances look in clients?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It can affect presentation of names and amounts, so we should decide deliberately. We'll set both convention-change selectors to No One. Pausing transfers, freezing one holder, and changing presentation are three separate choices; none should be inferred from the others.

scenes.title: Marketplace and direct-pricing permissions
scenes.screen: Marketplace Trade Mode Change and Direct Purchase Pricing Change actor/admin. Keep owner performer / No One admin for final example; no direct sale submitted.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Do these marketplace and pricing rules put CloudPoint on sale immediately?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. Marketplace Trade Mode Change controls who may change marketplace eligibility. Direct Purchase Pricing Change controls who may set or change direct-purchase pricing. Neither publishes a sale or chooses a price here.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: An owner-managed reward token could retain those powers for a later sale, while a giveaway token might forbid them?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. We'll retain both performers as Contract Owner and set their administrators to No One. Remember, marketplace eligibility is separate from normal transfers between holders.

scenes.title: Main control group changes
scenes.screen: Main Control Group Change dropdown and conditional identity/group inputs. Restore No One. Point toward Groups section next.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does Main Control Group Change create the group that will govern our token?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No, it chooses who may replace the contract's main control group. No One disables that change. Other choices refer to owner, identity, or group authority.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If a group-position field appears, do I put an identity identifier there?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Use the group's actual position inside this contract, not an identity identifier or a group nickname. We'll create a small group next so those references become concrete. After the experiment, our final example will have no group, no main-group position, and main-control-group changes disabled.

scenes.title: A two-person group
scenes.screen: Groups -> Add New Group -> expand Group 0. Use the two member rows already created; do not click Add Member here. Set two distinct public identity IDs, each Power 1, Required Power 2, Main Control Group Position 0. No group action broadcast.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Click Add New Group and expand Group zero. Two member rows already exist: the owner and a second row to fill. We don't need Add Member yet.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: For a two-person treasury, we use two distinct public identity identifiers, power one each, and Required Power two?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. Both members are needed to reach that threshold. Zero is this group's position within the contract. Set Main Control Group Position to zero if this is to be the main group.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does that assign all token permissions to it?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. Each relevant action must explicitly reference this group. We're only defining membership and the threshold here.

scenes.title: Editing and assigning a group
scenes.screen: Add one temporary third member row, then Remove Member. Show action performer Group 0 / Main Group. Restore owner-based action rules, clear group references and main position, then Remove This Group. End with no group and blank main position.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Now can we try adding a third member without changing the two-person example?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Add one temporary row, then Remove Member to remove it. Keep the threshold reachable: two required power with one power-one member wouldn't work.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Where do we assign the group to an action?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The performer selector now offers Group zero and Main Group. Choose the reference intentionally, then decide who can change that action rule.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And our final cleanup?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Restore the owner-based rules, clear group references and the main position, and use Remove This Group to delete the practice group. We'll verify that no hidden references remain.

scenes.title: Distribution controls: what they do
scenes.screen: Distribution, enable/disable Perpetual, Pre-Programmed, Once-per-identity. Explain practice-preview status and final all-off policy.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Are these distribution settings different ways to deliver the Initial Supply?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: They describe additional allocations. Perpetual Distribution uses recurring periods and an emission function. Pre-Programmed Distribution lists scheduled allocations to specific identities. Once Per Identity offers one claim per identity when the network supports it.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If a period passes, will tokens automatically appear in my wallet?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Recurring and scheduled entitlements are collected through the appropriate Claim action. A schedule isn't an invisible transfer running on this computer. We'll inspect example recipes, not perform claims, and all three systems will be off in the final CloudPoint registration. Their change permissions will be locked too.

scenes.title: Choose the period
scenes.screen: Enable perpetual; Time-Based, Epoch-Based, Block-Based selectors; interval numeric and unit dropdown. Small examples one day, one epoch, ten blocks.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Enable Perpetual Distribution. Time-Based measures a duration with a unit; one day will be our main example.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Why might I choose Epoch-Based or Block-Based instead?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Epoch-Based follows Platform epochs. Don't assume a fixed number of clock hours. Block-Based follows block counts: ten blocks is a count, not a guaranteed wall-clock duration.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: The function then provides an amount for each of those periods?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Choose the period that matches the policy you intend. We'll show one day, one epoch, and ten blocks to distinguish the inputs, then return to one-day periods for the ordinary worked recipes.

scenes.title: Recipients and emission units
scenes.screen: Recipient selector: owner, specific identity, evonodes. Only pair Evonodes with Epoch-Based. Base-units overlay for decimals=2.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can recurring emissions go somewhere other than the owner?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Choose Contract Owner, a Specific Identity, or the evonode recipient category. Evonodes requires Epoch-Based distribution; selecting it with another interval doesn't make that combination valid. Our ordinary examples use the owner or a named treasury.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Are these amounts entered like Base Supply?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Here's the important difference: emission amounts use base units. With two decimals, one thousand base units means ten tokens. The Supply fields scale displayed token amounts; these distribution parameters don't all use that widget. Keep the units overlay visible as we change functions. A familiar-looking number can represent a different amount here.

scenes.title: Read the emission examples
scenes.screen: Function selector and information button/formula view. Overlay k and base-unit conventions; no registration.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The Function selector determines the amount for each period. Information buttons explain formulas, and our tables show small worked examples in base units.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can I treat minimum, maximum, and trailing amount as interchangeable safeguards?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No, each changes a particular part of the calculation. We'll name every parameter we enter rather than copying a curve by appearance.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And Start Period Offset means a delay after registration?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Don't read it that way. It isn't simply a number of days to wait. We'll leave the optional start field empty in these recipes and use this build's precise interpretation.

scenes.title: Period indices and the first five periods
scenes.screen: Period-index overlay k=0..5, Initial Supply shown separately. One-day interval, owner recipient, precision2. No live claim promise.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Our table begins at k equals zero. Is that an extra allocation at registration?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. Initial Supply is separate. Here k measures the period index from the registration period, with the optional start field empty. We include zero to illustrate the formula.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Which values contribute over five eligible periods?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: One through five, excluding the starting boundary and including the end. Network period indices determine those boundaries. Don't interpret the table as a stopwatch promising a first claim exactly twenty-four hours after Confirm.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So these are calculation examples, not five payments we've already made.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. No claim is being performed here.

scenes.title: FixedAmount
scenes.screen: FixedAmount, Fixed Amount per Interval100. Overlay k0..5:100 each; five-period sum500=5.00tokens.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Choose FixedAmount and enter one hundred in Fixed Amount per Interval. Each period contributes one hundred base units, or one token at two decimals.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Five eligible periods would contribute five hundred base units: five tokens?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Before other applicable restrictions, yes. A fixed recurring treasury allowance is a straightforward use for this recipe.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does fixed mean the total token supply is fixed too?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Only the recurring amount is fixed here. Supply limits and permission rules are separate settings, and Claim still matters.

scenes.title: StepDecreasing
scenes.screen: StepDecreasing. StepCount2, numerator1, denominator2, startblank, initial100, minimum10, maxintervalcount3, trailing10. Overlay f0..8=100,100,50,50,25,25,12,12,10.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: How would we taper a reward toward a small continuing allowance?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Choose StepDecreasing. Set Step Count two, Decrease Numerator one, and Denominator two. That fraction is removed each reduction, leaving half. Leave the start field empty; use initial amount one hundred, minimum ten, maximum interval count three, and trailing amount ten.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What sequence should the table show?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: One hundred twice, fifty twice, twenty-five twice, twelve twice, then ten. Maximum Interval Count limits reduction eras, not individual days. The trailing branch begins after that era count is exceeded.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does the minimum automatically raise the trailing amount?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. The trailing value is a separate choice.

scenes.title: Stepwise
scenes.screen: Select Stepwise. Ensure exactly three rows, accounting for the initial empty row; add only missing rows. Set Start Step/Amount 0:10, 3:5, 5:0. Add and remove one extra practice row. Overlay f(0..6)=10,10,10,5,5,0,0.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Stepwise gives us an explicit table. Ensure there are exactly three rows: start zero, amount ten; start three, amount five; start five, amount zero.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So the latest start we've reached supplies the amount?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes: ten through index two, five at three and four, then zero. That stops future emissions; it doesn't erase existing balances.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can we add two rows with the same start to combine rewards?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: A duplicate index replaces an earlier value rather than adding another payment. Use at least two distinct starts. Add Step and Remove edit draft rows; we'll briefly add and remove an extra practice row. This suits a campaign with distinct reward phases.

scenes.title: Linear
scenes.screen: Linear a2,d1,sblank,b10,min0,max20. Overlay formula2k+10 clipped20; f0..5=10,12,14,16,18,20.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: For a reward rising by the same amount each period, should I choose Linear?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Set slope numerator a to two, divisor d to one, leave s empty, and set starting amount b to ten. Use minimum zero and maximum twenty.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: That gives ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, then stays at twenty?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Correct. The positive divisor controls the slope's scale. Negative slopes can model a decline, with deliberate bounds.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Is maximum twenty our token supply limit?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It's the function's per-period maximum. Max Supply is the separate ceiling on outstanding token supply.

scenes.title: Polynomial
scenes.screen: Polynomial a1,m2,n1,d1,sblank,o1,b0,min0,max100. Overlay (k+1)^2; f0..5=1,4,9,16,25,36.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Polynomial supports a power curve. Enter a one, m two, n one, d one; leave s empty. Set argument offset o one, added amount b zero, minimum zero, maximum one hundred.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: With m divided by n as the exponent, that's k plus one, squared?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes: one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five, thirty-six. The offset changes the input inside the power; b adds to the result.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What if the exponent is fractional, or just one?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Fractional powers involve rounding. A positive exponent of one belongs in Linear. Use accelerating rewards only deliberately, with their cost bounded; the curve doesn't make that decision for us.

scenes.title: Exponential
scenes.screen: Exponential a10,m1,n1,d1,sblank,o0,b0,min0,max100. Overlay 10exp(k), floor/clamp; f0..5=10,27,73,100,100,100.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does Exponential use powers of two?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The natural exponential uses base e. It can also describe decline. Set a ten, m one, n one, d one; leave s empty. Set o and b to zero, minimum zero, maximum one hundred.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What does that produce?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Ten, twenty-seven, seventy-three, then one hundred as the bound takes effect. The m-over-n ratio scales the exponent; d divides the result, o shifts its input, and b adds an amount. Positive growth requires a maximum here.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Much faster growth than our linear example.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. I enjoy an elegant curve, but my enthusiasm isn't an emission budget.

scenes.title: Logarithmic
scenes.screen: Logarithmic a10,d1,m1,n1,sblank,o1,b10,min0,max100. Overlay floor(10ln(k+1))+10; f0..5=10,16,20,23,26,27.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can we keep increasing a reward while slowing its growth?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Logarithmic can do that. Set a ten, d one, m one, n one; leave s empty. Use o one, b ten, minimum zero, maximum one hundred.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What happens to the first outputs?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Ten, sixteen, twenty, twenty-three, twenty-six, twenty-seven. This uses the natural logarithm of k plus one. The offset keeps the starting input positive.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Do m and n form a power exponent here too?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: They scale the logarithm's input, despite the generic form label. The logarithmic part is rounded down before b is added.

scenes.title: InvertedLogarithmic
scenes.screen: InvertedLogarithmic a10,d1,m1,n1,sblank,o1,b40,min0,max100. Overlay floor(10ln(1/(k+1)))+40; f0..5=40,33,29,26,23,22.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: InvertedLogarithmic takes the logarithm of a reciprocal. Keep a ten, d one, m one, n one, s empty, o one; change b to forty, with minimum zero and maximum one hundred.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What values should we see?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Forty, thirty-three, twenty-nine, twenty-six, twenty-three, twenty-two. Rounding the negative logarithmic part down gives thirty-three rather than thirty-four.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Is the formula one divided by a logarithm?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. The reciprocal is inside the logarithm: n above m times the shifted period. This example declines toward a zero floor. All eight functions are alternatives; selecting one doesn't run the others alongside it.

scenes.title: Intervals, bounds and recipe checks
scenes.screen: Show all six Time Unit entries: Second, Minute, Hour, Day, Week, Year. No Month entry. Restore one Day. Explain whole-minute alignment, including the one-Year exception. Open the static information illustration, then close it. Compare blank optional bounds with zero; reset to FixedAmount 100 for the permission tour.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Which time units are actually available?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, and years. They are fixed multipliers, not a calendar scheduler. There's no Month option in this build.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does every selectable interval pass network validation?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: No. Supported time intervals must align to whole minutes; one second fails. The year multiplier also makes one year fail that alignment. We'll use the verified one-day example. Epoch and block intervals have their own constraints.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And the help illustration follows my current parameters?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: It's static explanatory artwork. An empty optional bound can mean no bound; zero has field-specific meaning. Consult the parameter table for these and offsets. Random isn't a selectable function here.

scenes.title: Changing recurring emissions
scenes.screen: Expand the single Perpetual Distribution Rules section. Demonstrate performer, administrator and three switches; explain that it covers configuration including recipient. Set both selectors No One and all three switches false before disabling perpetual distribution. Do not show or imply a separate recipient-change panel.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Could we allow changes to the emission formula while separately locking its recipient?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: This creator offers one Perpetual Distribution Rules section for changes to the recurring configuration, including its recipient. There isn't a separate recipient-change rule. Whoever may change that configuration can potentially affect both.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: So we should review the performer, administrator, and three switches as a single policy.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. For our final token, set both selectors to No One and all three switches off while perpetual distribution is still enabled. Then turn it off.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Lock first, hide second, just like the default mint destination rule.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. The hidden settings still matter.

scenes.title: A scheduled allocation
scenes.screen: Perpetualoff. PreProgrammedon, Days1,Hours0,Minutes0,realpublicIdentity,Amount250. AddsecondrowDays2,Amount100; removesecond. No submit.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: With perpetual distribution off, enable Pre-Programmed Distribution. Enter one day, zero hours, zero minutes, a public recipient identity, and amount two hundred fifty: two and a half tokens at two decimals.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can I add another allocation for two days and one hundred base units?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Use Add New Distribution Entry, then Remove it after the example. Distinct time or recipient matters; identical timestamp-and-identity keys can overwrite an earlier amount.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Does one day mean exactly a day after registration completes?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: The timestamp is calculated when the form parses, and reopening preview can recalculate it. The recipient later uses Claim. Remove practice entries and disable this feature afterward.

scenes.title: Once per identity
scenes.screen: OncePerIdentity featuregateifavailable; Amount100; info; finaloff. If unavailable show disabled reason and labeled instructional callout instead of pretending enabled.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Would Once Per Identity Distribution make a giveaway limited to one claim per person?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Per identity, not per person. A user can control several identities. This feature isn't proof of personhood.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: When can we configure it?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: This build requires a known supported protocol version of at least fourteen. If unavailable, we'll show the disabled explanation and an instructional callout rather than pretend it's enabled. Amount one hundred means one token at two decimals when an eligible identity claims.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Is that claim guaranteed regardless of supply?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Available supply can still limit claims. We'll leave the feature off for our final registration.

scenes.title: Reset the emission practice
scenes.screen: Allthreeoff. No groups. DefaultdestinationOwner. Restore final actionrules using exactfinalconfigmanifest; overlay states tourvsfinal.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Before moving on, how do we distinguish our experiments from the token we'll actually publish?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Turn all three distribution systems off, keep their change rules locked, remove the practice group and its references, and restore the final owner-based rules. Collapsing a section isn't disabling it.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: CloudPoint should have one thousand initially, a permanent ten-thousand ceiling, two decimals, and ordinary transfers enabled?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. The owner may mint within the cap and burn its own balance. Freeze, unfreeze, and destruction of frozen funds stay disabled. Those eight emission recipes were examples, not eight registered tokens or completed claims. We'll inspect every authority again in JSON.

scenes.title: Document Schemas
scenes.screen: DocumentSchemas JSON note example from sidecar. Show parsegreen; malformedJSON localerror; restoreexample; ViewJSON constructiononly if successful. Clearfinal. No docscreated.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Would Document Schemas create documents automatically or let me upload a token logo?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Neither. It adds document types to the same data contract, without creating documents or changing balances. Our example defines a note type with required text, maximum length one hundred twenty, and no extra properties.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: What do I paste: a complete contract or a document?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: A map of type names to schemas. The green parse message confirms basic field structure, not full Platform acceptance. We'll show a malformed JSON error, restore the example, and inspect construction only if it succeeds. Developers must validate the full contract. Clear this field for our final token.

scenes.title: View JSON
scenes.screen: ViewJSON, scroll, resize, rawamounts and permissions; Close/X/Escoutside behavior briefly. Save approved final snapshot to artifacts, no editimport claim.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: View JSON builds a contract preview without registering it. Scroll or resize the window; Close, the cross, Escape, or an outside click dismisses it.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Can I edit it and import those changes here?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: This view has no JSON import or copy button. Check that decimals is two. Base supply should be one hundred thousand and maximum supply one million, both expressed in base units.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Then check recipient, transferability, histories, distributions, and every performer and administrator?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly, including hidden rules. Save the approved configuration for review, but not its identifier as the final Contract ID. Registration rebuilds the contract, so the preview identifier is temporary.

scenes.title: Final advanced authority review
scenes.screen: Show the exact final manifest and spotlight actual rules, then JSON. Mint/Burn/Emergency/Marketplace/Pricing performers Contract Owner; Freeze/Unfreeze/Destroy/Max Supply/Conventions performers No One; Main Control Group Change No One. Every rule administrator No One; every later-rule-change flag false. New Tokens Destination Identity Rules, Minting Allow Choosing Destination Rules and Perpetual Distribution Rules all No One/No One/false. No groups; all distributions off. Default mint recipient owner; per-mint recipient choice true. Preserve supply 1000/max 10000, decimals 2, unpaused, transferable, six histories enabled, English CloudPoint/CloudPoints, blank additional keywords and document schemas.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Let's state the final permissions together before we sign anything.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Owner: mint within the hard cap, burn its own tokens, pause or resume, manage marketplace eligibility, and manage direct-purchase pricing. No One: freeze, unfreeze, destroy frozen funds, change maximum supply or conventions, and change the main control group.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Every rule administrator No One, and every later-rule-change switch off, including nested rules?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes: destination-policy changes and perpetual-distribution changes are locked too. All distributions are off and no groups remain. Default mint recipient is the owner; individual mint recipients may still be chosen. These are explicit owner powers. Change any unsuitable choice before registration.

scenes.title: Register CloudPoint
scenes.screen: RegisterTokenContract confirmation; actualvalues estimate; CanceloneillustratedreviewthenConfirmlastonce. Waitrealresult savedpublicreceipt. No fabricatedsuccess.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Click Register Token Contract and compare the confirmation with our final plan. The compact dialog doesn't repeat every advanced permission; that's why we inspected JSON.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: The estimated fee still comes from the identity's Platform credits, with a Dash equivalent displayed?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Keywords and distribution features can affect that estimate. It isn't the price of CloudPoint or an exact receipt. If something differs, Cancel, correct the draft, and review it again.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Then Confirm once and wait for the actual result.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. We will show the observed outcome and verify the token in My Tokens. Submission and confirmed registration are different states.

scenes.title: Verify and recover
scenes.screen: Successonlyifobserved, MyTokens refresh, selectedtokenbalance1000, MoreInfo publicIDs. If failure actualmessage pause production and fix; do not narrate hypotheticalsuccessasdone.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: After confirmed success, I'll refresh My Tokens if needed and inspect CloudPoint. We expect one thousand tokens in the creator identity because the default recipient is the owner.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Right. Save the full Token ID and Contract ID from the result. Registration hasn't already performed a later mint, burn, freeze, or sale merely because we configured permissions for some of those actions.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: If the request is slow or the result unclear, should I check existing token and contract state before retrying?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Yes. Read the actual error and correct its cause. Don't create another paid contract just because the response outlasted my attention span.

scenes.title: Closing
scenes.screen: Official Dash Evolution closing slide 1920x1080. Display Chad G. P. Taylor and Ewa Dashwood; captions and AI-generated narration notice. Credit official logo through the linked companion page.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I started by asking which choices become permanent. Now I'd check who can act, who can change the rules, and whether the final configuration matches the policy we described.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: That's the useful habit. We've covered simple creation, advanced permissions, groups, all eight emission functions, scheduled and once-per-identity allocations, document schemas, and registration checks.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: And the chapters and parameter tables let us revisit a recipe before using it.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.text: Exactly. I'm Chad G. P. Taylor. Thanks for joining us. May your token policies be more carefully tested than my confidence, which remains the least thoroughly audited system in this tutorial.
